The Sandy sprat (Hyperlophus vittatus) is a small, pelagic clupeiform fish endemic to the coastal waters of southern Australia. This species exhibits a relatively rapid life history, with yolk-sac larvae emerging from the incubating eggs after a brief incubation period. At a consistent water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time from fertilisation through chorion rupture to the emergence of the prolarva is approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other small-bodied clupeids under similar thermal regimes. The larval stage is notably short, and upon reaching the juvenile transition, individuals begin a period of rapid somatic growth. Field surveys and captive rearing studies have documented that the maximum recorded body length, or ultimate length, attained by adult Sandy sprat reaches 10 cm [Li = 10 cm], a modest size consistent with its position as a forage fish in the pelagic food web. This length is typically achieved after several months of sustained feeding on zooplankton, with growth rates modulated by seasonal fluctuations in prey availability.

Reproductive development in the Sandy sprat is tightly coupled with thermal conditions. At the same experimental temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the age at which an individual reaches puberty and becomes capable of vitellogenesis and spermiation onset has been estimated at 5.8 cm [Lp = 5.8 cm] in terms of oozoid length at puberty. This morphological benchmark corresponds to a substantial investment in somatic tissue before reproductive activation, as the wet weight at puberty has been measured at approximately 0.94 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.94 grams]. This value was derived from morphometric relationships established during the species' growth trajectory. The transition from an immature post-metamorphic juvenile to a sexually mature adult is thus marked by both a specific length and a concomitant increase in body mass, reflecting the energetic requirements of gonad maturation. Comparative data from other clupeiform fishes indicate that such a size at puberty is typical for a species that matures within its first year of life.

The daily reproductive output of Sandy sprat has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. For a female at a fork length of 87 mm, the estimated number of eggs per spawning event is approximately 5600 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 5600 eggs] with a frequency of approximately one spawning every 65 days [F_R_i = approximately one spawning every 65 days], providing a robust estimate of fecundity for this size class, equivalent to a reproductive rate at FL 87 mm of approximately 15.34 eggs per day  at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This reproductive output was determined by averaging total egg counts from multiple spawning events over a 365-day period, and it varies with female size, age, and nutritional condition. The value represents a peak reproductive capacity, as larger, older individuals are capable of sustained spawning activity. This elevated rate is a key component of the species' life history strategy, enabling rapid population replenishment in the dynamic coastal environment where Sandy sprat is a critical link in the trophic web.

Neonatal body mass is an important parameter for understanding early life stage survival. The wet weight at birth for Sandy sprat, based on extrapolation from the length-mass relationship at the oozoid length at puberty, is approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This extremely small mass is typical of pelagic marine fish larvae that rely on a yolk-sac for endotrophic nutrition before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The body mass of a fully grown adult contrasts starkly with this birth weight. The ultimate wet weight recorded for the species, representing the maximum attainable mass in adults, is 44.6 grams [Wwi = 44.6 grams], a value that underscores the considerable size increase from the larval stage and aligns with the typical body mass of small, schooling planktivores in the region. This value was derived from the assumption of a spherical egg with a diameter of 0.9 mm at the point of spawning, integrating the species' maximum size with its reproductive physiology. The five orders of magnitude increase from birth to adulthood underscores the high growth potential of this small pelagic fish.

Lifespan in the Sandy sprat is relatively compressed, reflecting a pattern common among small, schooling forage fishes. Under stable thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum documented longevity for this species is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, as individuals typically mature within their first year and can spawn repeatedly. The species is considered iteroparous, with adults capable of multiple spawning events across their lifetime. Longevity records are derived from both field-based otolith ageing studies and observations of captive populations, which show a sharp increase in natural mortality after the fourth year. Factors such as predation pressure from larger piscivorous fish and seabirds, coupled with the energetic demands of sustained reproduction, likely contribute to this relatively short lifespan. In comparison to other clupeids of similar body size, the 5-year maximum lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] places Sandy sprat at the moderate end of the spectrum for its family at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].
